title: Down the Southern Slope
story:
Cloudveil Pass did not hold James for long; the wind on the crest was sharp and restless, urging him forward into the unknown. With the strap of Barnaby's canister adjusted across his chest, he took his first purposeful steps down the mountain's southern face. Behind him lay Oakhaven, the Grand Library, and the safe, familiar nooks of his recent days, but before him lay a landscape entirely unmapped by his charcoal.

Down through the drifting mountain fog, down along the slick spine of slate and granite, down toward the wide green basin below, the narrow trail guided his descent. The air grew richer and damper with every switchback, smelling faintly of ancient cedar, wet ferns, and cold river stones. James checked the small brass pocket compass nestled against his palm; its dark needle quivered reliably, keeping him pointed true toward the south as the mist swirled around his ankles.

By early afternoon, the clouds gathered close and let fall a soft, steady highland drizzle. Rather than retreat, James paused beneath the sheltering bough of a towering highland pine, watching the rainwater bead and slide along the colorful threads Mateo had woven around his canister strap. Through gaps in the descending cloud bank, he caught breathtaking glimpses of the Highland Terraces—vast, green-stepped hillsides carved into the mountains centuries ago, rising gracefully out of the deep valley.

He continued down until the rugged dirt trail met an ancient path of flat river stones, worn smooth by countless generations of travelers. Stepping onto an arched stone terrace overlook jutting out above the valley, James listened to the rhythmic drip of moisture falling from broad fern fronds onto the rock. The town he had known was completely hidden by the ridge behind him, yet here, standing on wet stone beneath the quiet canopy of rain, the wider world felt neither empty nor unkind.
